⚖️ New this morning: The FTC sent civil subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic yesterday seeking documents about safety incidents that have spiraled into an industry crisis, Axios' Maria Curi scoops.
 
 
1 big thing: Chuck's final fight
 
Sen. Schumer (D-N.Y.) sounds the alarm on Flock surveillance cameras in Manhattan on Oct. 4. Photo: Ron Adar/SOPA Images via Reuters

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is on the cusp of leading his party to midterm victory and reclaiming his title as Senate majority leader.

  • Winning the majority isn't a done deal. But this son of Brooklyn, who has been in public life for 52 years, is more than favored to win a secret ballot to remain Democratic leader, Axios' Hans Nichols writes.

Why it matters: At age 75 (76 by the time the new Congress convenes in January), Charles Ellis Schumer, an old-school pol who visits all 62 of New York's counties every year, looks poised to do what very few people do in life — go out on top.

🏛️ Behind the scenes: For starters, Democratic senators aren't quietly maneuvering — or publicly positioning themselves — to take the top job, according to senior aides. You can't beat someone with no one.

  • A handful of Democratic Senate candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, haven't committed to supporting Schumer for leader. But they likely don't have the votes to stage a coup. And Schumer's super PAC is spending heavily to get them across the line.

That calculus could change if Republicans overperform expectations with a massive win, potentially triggering a serious leadership challenge.

  • Otherwise, the job is Schumer's for the asking — and he's asking. "I am running for re-election for leader. Period," he said two weeks ago.

🗽 The intrigue: The bigger question surrounding Schumer involves 2028 and whether he'd retire at the top of his game or risk an embarrassing primary loss to, perhaps, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was born in the Bronx and represents parts of the Bronx and Queens.

  • If Schumer decided to retire, he could spend his final two years in leadership, freed from the political pressures that have defined his career.

That would give Senate Republicans and President Trump an entirely new political animal to contend with: YOLO Chuck.

  • Republican YOLO senators (with nothing left to lose, since You Only Live Once) have been playing hardball with President Trump. But it's unclear how a YOLO Chuck would act as majority leader.

💡 Between the lines: Schumer finds himself in a position remarkably similar to that of the man he'd replace: Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

  • Both are distrusted by their parties' most vocal activists. The insults hurled at them — weak, coward, sellout — are almost interchangeable.
  • But most of the criticism comes from outside the chamber. Behind closed doors, their caucuses are expected to close ranks.

The bottom line: If Schumer announces early in the next Congress that he won't seek another term as leader in 2028, Washington could find itself in an unusual position — with a term-limited president negotiating with a Senate majority leader who has nothing left to lose.

2. Musk's rescue mission
 

Photo illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photo: Marc Piasecki/Getty Images
 

Elon Musk, by far the biggest known midterm donor, is single-handedly keeping the Republican Party afloat in some of its most vital races.

  • Musk's team reached out to Republicans in late August to discuss a train wreck they all saw coming: Unless the GOP poured more money into Texas immediately, the state's Senate race could be lost in a matter of weeks, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reports.

Why it matters: That chat set in motion a massive rescue operation for Republican Ken Paxton funded substantially by Musk, the party's largest donor, who gave $158 million in September alone.

Musk's rescue gave Paxton's sleepy campaign new life and showed why the world's richest person is the X factor in the push to prevent a midterm debacle for President Trump's party.

  • It also helped Republicans avoid a death-spiral scenario: that propping up Paxton in Texas would force them to drain badly needed resources from other Senate battlegrounds.
  • Instead, Musk's money allowed Republicans to flood Texas' expensive TV markets and free up cash to shore up unexpectedly competitive races in Kansas and South Carolina.

🧮 By the numbers: Musk, the world's richest person, accounted for nearly 60% of the $273 million raised in Q3 by the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Senate Republicans.

  • Share this story.
Photo: CNN

📺 At the end of a 90-minute CNN/Jubilee town hall in Fort Worth last night, James Talarico, Texas Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, pointed out how civil and issue-oriented the conversation had been:

  • "You may have noticed that I haven't talked about my opponent at all tonight ... I don't want people to vote just against Ken Paxton. I want them to vote for me. I want them to know my values and my vision."
  • Talarico, 37, then hammered Paxton, 63, as "the most corrupt politician in Texas."

Moderator Erin Burnett said Paxton, the state attorney general, hadn't responded to an invitation for his own town hall.

3. 🤖 Anthropic gives Wall Street an AI bull case
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

AI companies for years have promised that smarter models would be worth the staggering cost to build them. Anthropic made that case last night in cash, Axios' Madison Mills writes.

  • The company presented eye-popping financials to investors, saying it was cash-flow positive in the third quarter, with revenue surging nearly 50% to $16.8 billion compared to the April-to-June period.

Why it matters: As Wall Street broadly spent the day fearing an AI bubble, Anthropic offered what investors have been desperate to see: evidence that frontier AI can be a sustainable business.

🔬 Zoom in: Consider just one of the stats reported by Anthropic: the company is cash-flow positive even as some of the world's most profitable companies are struggling to keep their AI spending in check.

  • For context, Google's parent, Alphabet, long a money-printing machine, turned free cash flow negative in its second quarter as AI infrastructure investment soared.

The big picture: Anthropic's early bets on coding expertise, business customers and spending discipline have paid off.

  • Claude Code, a viral hit that brought users to Anthropic in droves, reached an estimated annualized revenue of $6 billion to $7 billion by late summer, according to Bloomberg Intelligence.
  • Customers have generally been reluctant to switch once they've adopted it, according to PitchBook data.

🥊 Reality check: Anthropic still faces enormous training costs and stock-based compensation expenses, which could weigh on its underlying profitability.

  • And Anthropic faces more than $500 billion in planned infrastructure and computing spending over the next decade.

4. 📉 Charted: CEO mood sours
 
Data: The Conference Board and The Business Council. Chart: Axios/Emily Peck

CEO confidence in the U.S. economy sank into negative territory earlier this month, Axios' Emily Peck writes from a Conference Board survey out this morning.

  • The CEO Confidence Index — a survey of 131 Fortune 500 CEOs — fell to 46, down from 52 just three months ago. Any number below 50 signals negative sentiment.

⚠️ Threat level: 41% of CEOs expected economic conditions to worsen — up from 19% in the previous quarter.

  • Executives' concerns over cybersecurity, AI and geopolitics rose significantly from three months ago.

5. ⚡ Scoop: "OG" Bill Gates returns for AI fight
 

Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Getty Images
 

Bill Gates is gearing up to dramatically expand his AI safety push, personally leaning on business leaders and considering a major deployment of his resources, sources tell Axios' Bradley Olson.

Why it matters: The formidable, sharp-elbowed Bill Gates who built Microsoft is back. He's directing his competitive fire toward what he has come to see as one of the most important causes of his lifetime.

  • "I can reach CEOs on this better than you can," Gates told one person he consulted on AI safety, showing an eagerness for combat that associates say is a return to "OG" form.

🔬 Zoom in: Once a voice for optimism on AI, Gates has grown dismayed by an escalation of model capabilities, alarming security incidents and what he sees as insufficient regulation, sources say.

  • As he prepared to make the case for a far more robust regulatory framework on AI, he consulted extensively with leading AI executives, researchers, and safety advocates, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

Behind the scenes: People Gates has spoken to called his advocacy a "comeback tour," an attempt to rebuild a legacy that has been tarnished by his past association with Jeffrey Epstein.

  • Gates has said he's aware that some people may dismiss his warnings due to the Epstein ties.
  • But he sees the stakes as too high to stay on the sidelines and believes his Rolodex, foundational tech credibility and wealth can do an immense amount of good.

🔮 What's next: Gates' calls for robust regulation will put him on a collision course with the Trump administration, which has favored a lighter regulatory touch.

6. 🪖 America's not ready for space war
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Axios' Thomas Novelly writes in the inaugural SPACE edition of our Future of Defense newsletter, out this morning:

The future of war is in outer space — and the U.S. is unprepared for the fallout.

  • Why it matters: An outbreak of space warfare would cripple the global economy by disrupting satellites used for everything from worldwide financial transactions to maritime navigation. It would also hinder the U.S. military's ability to conduct some of its key missions on Earth.

The dependence on satellites is precisely what makes them tempting targets for foes.

  • China has made major advancements, including satellites with robotic arms that could disable U.S. equipment and lasers that can blind military space sensors.
  • Russia lags behind, but U.S. officials fear Moscow may unleash an orbital nuclear weapon that "could pose a threat to all satellites and to the space-enabled services the world depends on."

💥 Threat level: Last month, U.S. officials revealed that the military had weapons in space — a bombshell admission they said was aimed at deterring adversaries.

  • Aerospace analysts warn the nation isn't prepared if China or Russia destroys U.S. satellites. They say the defense industry lacks the critical supplies and personnel to fight back.

7. 🐴 NYC reins in carriages
 
A horse-drawn carriage takes passengers for a loop through Central Park yesterday. Photo: Yuki Iwamura/AP

New York City lawmakers plan to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, ending their more than 150-year run as an iconic, old-timey tourist attraction.

  • Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the City Council speaker on the legislation that would end the rides by 2028.

The deal comes after decades of opposition from animal welfare activists and the death of a teenage tourist last spring.

8. 🖼️ 1 for the road: Apple's new era
 

Cover: TIME
 

Apple CEO John Ternus — who took over for Tim Cook last month — is on the cover of TIME's annual "Best Inventions" issue with an iPhone Duo.

  • The $1,999-and-up phone unfolds to the size of an open passport and will be released to the public a week from tomorrow.
Data: Financial Modeling Prep. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios
